title: Why a Test Can't Tell You Your 'Biological Age'
description: There's no simple number that can reveal the full truth about your health.
fullText:
It's not enough to live forever—everybody wants to stay young forever, too. In most wellness spaces, "youth" is a word that gets thrown around as synonymous with "health," but you don't have to be into woo-woo wellness culture to find yourself tempted to find out how old—or more accurately, how young—you really are. Maybe you can't fight your chronological age, but you can find comfort in an alternative framing: "biological age."

The pitch is appealing. Send in a vial of blood or a tube of spit, pay several hundred dollars, and receive a number that supposedly reveals your "true" biological age. The promise is that this age is the one your body is actually living, as opposed to the one on your driver's license. If you find out you're "biologically" 35 instead of 45, the implication is that you've pulled one over on the passage of time. Discover the reverse, and the tests often come bundled with supplements, programs, or subscriptions designed to fix your problems.

The real problem is that biological age isn't actually a single figure that can be measured or calculated, and no test—however promising the science behind it—can hand you a definitive verdict on how your body is aging. Here's what's actually going on inside these tests, what legitimate research says about aging, and how to think about the growing market of products promising to quantify your youth.

Chronological age is easy: you count the years since you were born. Biological age is an attempt to pin down how well your body is actually functioning relative to that timeline. Dr. Dan Belsky, an epidemiologist at Columbia University who studies aging, explains it this way: Everyone moves through calendar time at the same rate, but "the conditions inside our body obviously vary." Because health tends to decline over time, biological age is essentially an estimate of the age at which a person's physiological integrity—how well their organs and tissues function, resist stress, and recover from injury—would be considered typical within some reference group.

That last part is key. "There really is no ground truth biological age, because it's always relative to some expectation," Belsky says. Saying you're "biologically 25" only means something once you know what factors you're being judged on, and what standards you're being compared to. A biological age score is a construct built from a specific reference population, which could be a large, nationally representative sample, or a much smaller research cohort. That detail is key to understanding how much weight any individual result should carry.

Consumer biological age tests love to reduce aging to a single number, but researchers who study aging combine many types of data to get anywhere close to a meaningful picture. That typically includes laboratory-based biomarkers, like the kind of bloodwork your doctor might order during an annual physical. Those biomarkers are then placed alongside clinical measurements like blood pressure, heart rate, and imaging. Increasingly, researchers also look at molecular and cellular markers, including genes and proteins.

One of the most talked-about approaches in recent years uses "epigenetic clocks," which look at chemical modifications to your DNA (rather than the DNA sequence itself) and compare the pattern to population averages to estimate biological age. Several companies now sell consumer versions of this technology, generally priced around $300, using blood or saliva samples.

According to Belsky, at their best, these commercial tests are "a consumer implementation of a research tool." In practice, that means a lab takes an algorithm developed using a specific research dataset and applies it to your individual sample. The algorithm was built to describe patterns across groups, not to diagnose an individual person, which is part of why a single test result can deliver an unreliable personal verdict.

When it comes to what actually shapes biological aging, the answer is "almost everything," Belsky says. Genetics play a role in how resilient a person's body is over time. But environmental and behavioral factors are often just as important, if not more so. The quality of the water you drink and the air you breathe, your diet, and the stability and meaningfulness of your social relationships are critical. Sleep, exercise, and nutrition tend to dominate the public conversation, and for good reason, but they're part of a much longer list of contributing factors.

This is also where biological age intersects with inequality. Research has consistently linked poverty, pollution, and unstable living conditions to accelerated biological aging and shorter lifespans. Not everyone has equal access to fresh food, clean air, safe housing, or reliable medical care—and those disparities show up in the body over time. A biological age test can't account for the structural conditions someone is navigating; it can only reflect the downstream biological signal.

This is where the marketing gets ahead of the science. Many products claim you can measurably "reverse" your biological age through supplements, specific diets, or intensive protocols. The research, naturally, is more cautious. From the standpoint of how most people intuitively understand biological age (as a general reflection of your body's current state), yes, that state can be modified through better health habits. But whether behavioral, environmental, or pharmacological interventions actually change the pace of aging at the cellular level in humans? There we have "less clarity," Belsky says.

Of course, living a healthier life will generally support how your body functions, and likely influence the biomarkers that feed into these tests. But claims that a particular product has been shown to "reverse" cellular aging in a rigorous, replicated way should always be treated with skepticism. Despite the promises of certain longevity influencers, there's no evidence that any supplement, cold plunge protocol, or red light therapy device will add decades to your life.

It's also worth reframing the goal. Healthy aging isn't really about looking younger than your birth certificate suggests, or avoiding every illness. Instead, it could be more productive to think in terms of a broader health span: the stretch of life you spend active, capable, and free of major disability. That means building habits that help your body adapt as it inevitably changes with time, rather than wasting your time, money, privacy, and mental health in the pursuit of a lower number on a test result.

If you are itching to find out your "true" age, consider treating your score as a simple data point, as opposed to a catch-all verdict. "People often want a yardstick to track progress toward personal wellness goals," Belsky says, "and the best-evidenced tests have at least been studied in research settings, so there's some understanding of how their scores relate to disease risk, disability, mortality, and in some cases, how responsive they are to interventions." At the same time, "these are not standalone, one-shot measurements you can trust to reveal the full truth about your health." Like any biomedical test, they're subject to bias and error, and they need to be interpreted alongside other health information, ideally with a healthcare professional.

Before spending a few hundred dollars on a biological age test, it's worth asking yourself a more practical question: Let's say you find out your body is aging "faster" than your birthday suggests—how would you actually change your behavior? Perhaps a biological age test is the helpful nudge you need to jump-start habits you've been meaning to build anyway. But if you already generally know the factors that support long-term health—moving your body, eating well, sleeping enough, managing stress, maintaining relationships, avoiding smoking, and so on and so forth—maybe you can start making those changes today, no vial of blood required.

title: Your Fitness Tracker Has No Idea How Many Calories You’re Burning
description: It would be great if Fitbits and Apple Watches were accurate, but sorry—they're not.
fullText:
When I test smartwatches and fitness trackers, I place a particular emphasis on accuracy. Is my running pace correct? Does the device capture the ups and downs of my heart rate? I even got a VO2max lab test to check a bunch of watches' fitness scores. But one thing I never test for accuracy is calorie burn. None of my devices come close to agreeing on the number of calories they think I'm burning, and I don't expect them to. Even scientists who study the accuracy of wearables can't answer the question in a way that's useful when you're shopping for this year's devices—but we'll get into why that is below.

There was a time, before Fitbits, when nobody knew quite how many calories they were burning on a daily basis. Sure, you could calculate a rough estimate based on your body size, sex, and age. You could choose whether or not to believe the calorie readout on the cardio machines at the gym. (You shouldn't.) But the idea that a gadget on your wrist could tell you how many calories you personally burned during one particular day was revolutionary. It was also wrong.

Before I discuss how accurate fitness trackers are, let’s look at where they get their numbers. For calorie calculations, the main sources are motion and heart rate data. For motion, trackers use accelerometers to figure out when your body is moving, and by how much. If you have a watch on your wrist, and the watch swings back and forth rhythmically while sort of bouncing up and down, your gadget guesses that you must be walking. If there is quicker bouncing and your wrist makes a smaller movement, you’re probably running.

This is the basic idea behind how trackers detect how many steps you’re taking. If you’ve paid attention to your step count, you already know some of the ways this can be inaccurate. If you’re shopping, for example, keeping your hand on the shopping cart handle may result in you not getting credit for the steps you’re taking, though this depends on the device. (For a perfect illustration of this issue, see these tests I did comparing a Garmin to an Apple Watch on a treadmill. When I rested my hands on the treadmill handle, the Apple Watch recorded 318 steps while the Garmin recorded none.)

Then there’s the heart rate sensor: Since your hands don’t always move predictably during exercise, it can be easier to just tell your watch that you’ll be cycling or doing yoga or whatever. The gadget then uses your heart rate to make an educated guess about how much work your body is doing.

Whatever the source of the data—heart rate, movements, or a combination—the gadget processes it through a formula to calculate how many calories it thinks you’re burning. Your age, weight, and sex may figure into this equation. Importantly, though, the fitness tracker doesn’t actually know how many calories you’re burning; instead, it’s calculating a probable number based on incomplete information.

If humans were robots, all built the same, all moving in predictable patterns, this formulaic approach might work. But humans are complicated, and technology often gets confused. For example, you may get different step counts if you put a device on your right versus left wrist. And the optical heart rate sensors that a lot of trackers use may be less accurate on dark skin compared to lighter skin. These problems relate to the data that the trackers gather, but calorie burn isn't a direct measurement. It's an estimate derived from doing math with the data the watch measures, and different algorithms can come up with different calorie burn numbers depending on how the algorithm is designed.

The companies that make fitness trackers aren’t required to publish their algorithms or verify that their calorie counts are accurate. They can just put a device on the market, and there you are, comparing wearables on shopping sites without any information about how accurate they are, outside of the companies’ claims.

Researchers are interested in fitness trackers’ accuracy, which would seem like a good thing. They want to be able to use wearables in research or recommend them for individuals and healthcare providers, and so they'll run studies comparing consumer devices to lab equipment. This sounds like a great way to answer our questions! But there’s a huge delay in actually getting that information, and it’s often published too late to be useful. By the time a researcher buys a batch of the latest model, runs a study, writes it up, submits it to a journal, and finally gets it published, several years may have gone by, and the company has moved on to the next model.

That delay is why I (usually) can't use scientific studies to weigh in on the devices I write about. Here's a great example of how frustrating it can be: This review was published in 2025, and found the Series 1 was the Apple Watch that turned up the most often in the studies the authors were able to gather. The Series 9 and 10 watches were completely missing from the available data—and as a reminder, we're now up to the Series 12. With that caveat about delays, I still think it’s useful to look at the research on fitness trackers to see what themes emerge. Are any of them good at estimating your calorie burn?

Time for the bad news. A study from 2020 that looked at a variety of gadgets from Apple, Garmin, Polar, and Fitbit found that all the devices are inaccurate more often than they are accurate. The authors considered a device to be accurate if its reading was plus or minus 3% when compared to a more reliable measure of energy expenditure (that is, calorie burn) in a lab setting. Here’s how some of the top brands fared:

Garmin devices underestimated calorie burn 69% of the time.

Apple watches overestimated calorie burn 58% of the time.

Polar devices overestimated calorie burn 69% of the time.

Fitbits underestimated calorie burn 48% of the time and overestimated 39% of the time.

The fact that Fitbits were roughly correct on average doesn’t mean they were useful. If sometimes your device overestimates and sometimes it underestimates, it’s not very helpful unless you know which is which.

A 2018 review specifically of Fitbits found that accuracy varied greatly depending on factors like where they were worn (torso was more accurate than wrist), whether you were walking uphill, and whether you walked at a constant speed or stopped and started. The accuracy also varied by device, with the Fitbit Classic underestimating calorie burn and the Fitbit Charge usually overestimating. The devices just aren’t accurate enough to know how many calories you’re really burning

A 2022 study compared the Apple Watch 6, the Fitbit Sense, and the Polar Vantage V. The researchers had volunteers wear all three gadgets while sitting quietly, walking, running, cycling, and strength training. Every gadget, for every activity, was awarded a judgment of “poor accuracy,” with coefficients of variation ranging from 15% to 30%.

This 2025 review of Apple Watch studies—the same one I mention above—found that calorie burn was, on average, off by about 18%. The authors mention a proposed standard from the International Electrotechnical Commission that recommends fitness trackers not be off by more than 10%. That's clearly not being met, although the researchers noted that newer models may be more accurate than earlier ones.

And this 2026 study looked specifically at how accuracy relates to skin tone and to the amount of fat a person has. To the devices' credit, skin tone didn't seem to affect calorie counts very much, but adiposity (fat content) did. The higher a volunteer's body fat percentage was, the more inaccurate their calorie burn result. The Garmin Forerunner 955 and Samsung Galaxy Watch 5 seriously overestimated calories; the Apple Watch Series 8 also overestimated but not as much; and the Fitbit Sense 2 underestimated when it wasn't producing wild outliers. The authors concluded that all devices "substantially misestimate" calorie burn during exercise.

To get a sense of these percentages, let's say your true calorie burn is 2,000 calories per day. A device that's off by 15%—on the low end of what these studies found—might report that you burned 1,700 calories, or that you burned 2,300. If you're using your device to figure out how much to eat, you could be way off in meeting your calorie goals.

It’s probably most useful if you think of your calorie burn as a number you cannot measure directly. Treat it as a black box: I burn some unknowable number of calories; now what?

The only common reason you would need an accurate estimate of calorie burn is if you are trying to figure out how much food you need to eat. If you want to lose weight, you want to eat less than you burn; if you want to gain weight, you want the reverse; and if you’re trying to maintain your weight, you want to eat roughly the same as what you burn. But think about it this way: you don't actually need to know your calorie burn if you have the other two terms in the equation—your calorie intake and your weight.

It's considered more accurate to adjust how much to eat based directly on your weight, rather than using calorie burn estimates as a middleman. Let’s say you’re training for a marathon and you want to make sure you fuel yourself appropriately. Well, if you’re under-eating, you’ll start to lose weight. When you start to see the scale trending downward, that’s your signal to add a few hundred calories to your diet. If, after that adjustment, your weight stays steady, then you know you’re eating the right amount. As you increase your training (or if you take time off to rest a sprained ankle), you can make more adjustments as you go.

I have a post here detailing how to make these adjustments with the help of either a paid app, a group of free apps, or a DIY spreadsheet. If you’ve been using a fitness tracker instead, and it’s working for you, feel free to keep using it. But if the tracker ever stops giving you the results you want, you can safely leave it out of the equation.

title: Wales pick two father-son duos for Wheelchair World Cup squad
description: Fathers and sons Martin and Matthew Turner and Gareth Ramsey and Sid Ramsey are named in Wales' squad for the 2026 Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup.
fullText:
Wales have named two pairs of fathers and sons - Martin and Matthew Turner and Gareth and Sid Ramsey - in their squad for the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup in Australia.

It is the first time a father and son have represented Wales together at a Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup and the first time two such pairings have been named in one squad.

A father-and-son pair have featured in the Wales set-up previously, but never before on the World Cup stage.

Head coach Alan Caron included them in his 12-strong selection for the tournament, which starts for Wales against England on Friday, 30 October in Wollongong.

Group games against Ireland and the United States follow at the same venue as the teams aim for the knockout stages.

Gareth Ramsey, John Berriman and Fionn McCabe - who turns 16 shortly before the competition - could make Wales debuts during the event.

Caron said: "Having two father-and-son combinations in the squad makes this World Cup particularly special.

"Gareth and Sid, and Martin and Matthew, have the opportunity to share something that very few players ever get to experience: representing Wales together at a World Cup.

"For John, Fionn and Gareth, the opportunity to make their Wales debuts at a World Cup would be something very special, while our experienced players will be vital in helping them and the rest of the squad through the tournament."

Wales have had to fundraise to help with the costs of taking the squad to Australia, with more than half of the £10,000 target donated so far.

title: What have we learned from the Championship so far?
description: As we enter the three-week international break, BBC Sport looks back at the opening block of Championship fixtures to see what we have learned so far.
fullText:
After a gruelling 37-day slog the Championship has begun a near three-week break for international football.

What have we learned from the opening eight-game block of the marathon 46-game campaign?

Just seven points separate the top 15 sides in the Championship after eight games - though Wolves and Pompey have yet to play their game in hand which was postponed due to Carabao Cup clashes.

It already feels like it could be a fascinating season with no stand-out team as yet, and the table backs it up.

Swansea lead the way, QPR, Stoke, Bristol City and Charlton are in the chasing pack, and West Brom have swapped the bottom five last season for the top five this.

Interestingly, since the Championship adopted its current name in 2004, only once has a team topped the table after eight matches and had fewer than the 17 points the Swans have currently earned - indicating this is a wide-open league this year.

Brighton were top of the pile in 2012 with just 16 points but the Seagulls ended up finishing fourth and went on to lose in the play-offs.

Six other sides have been in first place with 17 points before the Swans, but only two of those - Leeds in 2019-20 and Sheffield United in 2022-23 - won promotion.

Sorry to break it to Swans fans, however, but three of the other four did not even finish in the top 10.

There have been 277 goals scored already in the Championship this season.

That's 36 more than at the same stage last season, with one fewer match having taken place, and the second most ever at this stage since the Championship rebrand in 2004-05.

What do we put it down to? Well the stats suggest it is due to more direct play and quality on the flanks.

Only once in the past nine seasons have more goals come from crosses than the 47 so far this campaign.

Also, 44 of those 47 have come from headers, the most at this stage by some distance over the past five seasons, while nine have come from throw-ins - the second most at this stage in the past 14 seasons, behind only last season's 12.

That suggests a real shift in the way the game has evolved in recent times, given that from 2013-14 to 2020-21, by this point of the campaign, just 14 goals across those eight seasons - an average of fewer than two - came from throw-ins.

Bristol City's on-loan Crystal Palace full-back Rio Cardines has six assists already, the most by any player in Europe's top leagues.

Burnley began this season aiming to do something which had never been done before - become a six-time yo-yo club.

Six of Sean Dyche's eight full seasons in charge of Burnley were in the Premier League, winning promotion in his first and third full campaigns, but since his departure in April 2022 and their subsequent relegation, they have not stayed still.

Under Vincent Kompany, they won the 2022-23 Championship title with 101 points - before being relegated with just 24 points the next year.

With Scott Parker they went up again with 100 points, only conceding 16 goals, but were relegated with four games remaining last season leading to Parker's exit.

Nicky Hayen was the man entrusted with trying to get the club back to the top tier, but it has been a tortuous start to life at Turf Moor.

After a summer of wholesale changes in the squad, Hayen was appointed just 29 days before the Clarets' first game - 75 days later, eight games, four points and no wins has the Clarets bottom of the Championship.

Fellow slow starters Preston, Cardiff and Derby - the Rams having rescued a last-gasp draw at Turf Moor on Saturday - are the only other sides to be averaging fewer than a point per game.

The bad news for Burnley fans is that no side has ever been promoted from the Championship having been without a win in their opening eight fixtures and of the past 10 occasions only one - Brentford in 2018 - went on to finish in the top half.

The slightly better news is that seven of them avoided relegation, including Portsmouth two years ago and Sheffield Wednesday the season before that.

Fresh from a summer adventure with World Cup co-hosts Canada, Saints striker Cyle Larin is setting a frightening pace in the race for the Golden Boot.

The 31-year-old has started every game this season having made his move from Mallorca permanent after scoring eight goals in 16 appearances on loan during the latter half of last season.

Larin's seven goals in eight games have come at an average of one every 85 minutes and have helped Saints overhaul their four-point penalty following 'Spygate'.

Middlesbrough's big-money signing from Tottenham, Will Lankshear, is one behind, with the 21-year-old one goal ahead of Norwich's Mo Toure, whose five goals have come from just 11 shots this season for one goal every 91 minutes on the pitch.

Tottenham fans may already be wondering if Lankshear might be the one who got away and you can be sure Premier League clubs will be keeping a close eye on proceedings in the second tier this season, given forwards are likely to prove better value and less risky than signings from other European leagues.

Toure, sadly, will not get chance to add to his tally any time soon - the Australia striker will be out for several months due to a shoulder injury sustained against Bolton on Sunday.

West Ham were the pre-season favourites for promotion, just ahead of Wolves and, ahem, Burnley.

The Hammers took a while to get going on their return to the second tier for the first time in 14 years and took two points from their opening three games, including a shock home defeat by Charlton.

They found their feet with four straight wins, culminating in a 6-0 demolition of Wrexham, before rolling up their sleeves to escape with a 2-2 draw in the derby at Millwall on Saturday, which left them in second place after Swansea's win later that day.

The Hammers' 22 goals across their opening eight league games is the most in 93 years and six of the past seven sides to score that many in the opening eight games have gone on to win the title.

Given the talent on the field and the depth of the squad there's nothing in the opening eight games to suggest the Hammers won't last the pace and make an immediate return to the top flight.

The same can be said of Wolves, who are just three points off the top, with that game against Portsmouth in hand.

Wanderers left it late to salvage a draw at home to Blackburn in the season opener but have found their feet and shrugged off a 4-2 defeat at West Ham to take seven points from their next three games, including the trip to Birmingham and the Black Country derby at home to West Bromwich Albion.

Given they won only three of their 38 league games and earned just 20 points in total last season, four wins and 14 points from seven matches with an overhauled squad is a fine start for new man Cesar Peixoto.

Who'd have had QPR among their promotion contenders after they finished last season with just two points from their final six matches?

The Hoops have the second best defensive record in the Championship with just seven goals conceded in their opening eight games and their only defeat came at home to Middlesbrough, in a game the R's might well have claimed a point or more.

Converting chances has been their biggest issue.

They have 261 touches in the opposition box, second most in the division, and won 55 corners, again second most, but their shot conversion rate of 7.3% is 20th of the 24 teams in the division.

After losing their first three games, Stoke have taken 13 points from the next five to sit just four points off the top.

Mark Robins was under immense pressure after taking one point from the final six games of last season to end up 17th, having been in the promotion race before Christmas, but things appear to be looking up for the Potters.

They are one point behind West Brom, who have swapped the bottom four last season for the top five this, despite losing to Wolves last time out.

Lincoln have returned to the second tier for the first time in 65 years with a new management team, and a bang.

Though they have the joint-lowest number of goals scored, the League One winners boast a division-best four clean sheets in eight games - along with Swansea - and their 11-point return from eight games has them just two points outside the top six, having widely been tipped to finish bottom.

title: GB boxers guaranteed three medals at Europeans
description: Britain guarantee at least three medals at the European Boxing Championships in Bulgaria as Chantelle Reid, Damar Thomas and Abdul Burton all reach the semi-finals.
fullText:
Great Britain are guaranteed at least three medals at the European Boxing Championships in Bulgaria after Chantelle Reid, Damar Thomas and Abdul Burton reached the semi-finals.

Reid cruised to a 5-0 win over Ireland's Evelyn Igharo in a women's light-middleweight contest at the Asics Arena Sports Hall in Sofia.

The 28-year-old Commonwealth Games silver medallist will face Serbia's Milena Matovic in the last four on Wednesday.

Thomas won by the same margin in a men's super-heavyweight fight against Georgia's Nikoloz Begadze and the 21-year-old will take on Mahammad Abdullayev of Azerbaijan in the semi-finals.

Burton, 20, beat home favourite and Olympic bronze medallist Javier Ibanez 3-2 to secure a meeting with Turkey's Semih Gumus.

"Sometimes you have got to dig in and when things went against me I had to get stuck in and show who I was," Burton said.

"I am young, hungry and here to take over."

Lauren Mackie, Amy Broadhurst, Callum Makin and Oladimeji Shittu are all due in quarter-final action on Wednesday, but over half of Britain's squad of 15 are now out.

On Tuesday, flyweight Ruby White was beaten 3-2 by Olympic silver medal winner Hatice Akbas of Turkey while Emily Asquith suffered a 5-0 defeat in her light-heavyweight bout with Ireland's Lisa O'Rourke.

In the men's heavyweight division, Commonwealth Games champion Isaac Okoh bowed out with a 3-0 defeat by Germany's Kevin Lebowski.

title: O'Neill receives Celtic backing after 'painful' week
description: Celtic will "come together and support" manager Martin O'Neill after a "painful" week for the club, says chief executive Michael Nicholson.
fullText:
Celtic will "come together and support" manager Martin O'Neill after a "painful" week for the club, chief executive Michael Nicholson has said.

O'Neill had indicated that he would use the international break to consider his future following two defeats to Rangers, either side of a home loss to Ferencvaros in the Europa League.

In the wake of Sunday's 1-0 derby defeat at Celtic Park, 74-year-old O'Neill had said "it might be time to wrap it up".

However, Nicholson suggested the club will rally round the manager who has delivered nine trophies over two spells.

His remarks came with the latest financial figures revealing a drop of nearly £33m in revenue.

A loss of £4.8m is largely down to the failure to reach last year's Champions League and Celtic have missed out again, squandering a 4-0 aggregate lead in their play-off with LASK last month.

"Having started well in the Premiership this season, we experienced disappointment in the Champions League play-off," said Nicholson in a written statement accompanying the financial results.

"Reaching the league phase of the Champions League is an objective for us all, and we are sorry not to have achieved it.

"On top of that, the losses in the last week have been painful for us all. We will now come together and support Martin and the players, as we focus our efforts on achieving success domestically and in the Europa League."

title: GB's Connor earns UFC contract despite defeat
description: Callum Connor wins a UFC contract after losing what Dana White describes as "one of the greatest fights you'll ever see".
fullText:
Britain's Callum Connor was given a UFC contract despite losing in Dana White's Contender Series, but Norbert Novenyi Jr missed out despite winning.

Six fighters from Tuesday's five fights earned contracts in MMA's leading promotion - four of the winners plus two losers, including 26-year-old Connor.

Peru's Piero Guaylupo earned a unanimous decision over lightweight rival Connor, who suffered the first professional loss of his career.

UFC president White said it could be a fight of the year contender because it contained more significant strikes than any UFC lightweight three-round bout.

"Both of these guys are in the hospital right now, as they should be," said White.

"One of the greatest fights you'll ever see on Tuesdays or Saturdays or any other day.

"For Piero to be 21 years old and fight the way he did, the fight was incredible. But it takes two guys to make a great fight. I'm taking them both."

Connor, from Manchester, now has a pro record of 8-1, including a four-fight win streak on UK promotion Full Contact Contender.

Middleweight Novenyi, who was born in Hungary but now fights out of London, earned a unanimous decision over American Theo Haig to improve his pro record to 11-1.

But the 26-year-old was the only fighter who won on Tuesday not to be given a contract. He was told by White that "tonight's not your night, my friend".

"Norbert, both of you guys have great records," White said. "You came in, fought a good fight.

"Unfortunately, I didn't see anything tonight that makes me say, 'I got to have this guy in the UFC'.

"Whatever you decide to do here, we would like to take another look at you."

title: 'Start-up' Newcastle tapping into Red Bulls spirit
description: Head coach Dan McFarland is excited to have the backing of Newcastle Red Bulls' owners as he tries to fuse a new team together in the Prem this season.
fullText:
It is all change at Newcastle Red Bulls as they prepare for the new Prem season, but they plan to tackle it with the sort of fearless approach for which their owners are renowned.

With Red Bull taking over at Kingston Park in August 2025, it was a scramble to get things in place for last season.

As a result, Newcastle could not bridge the gap to the other nine teams and finished bottom for a fourth successive campaign, with just two wins in 18 games.

But, after a huge influx of players in the summer, 'Red Bulls 2.0' under new head coach Dan McFarland are ready to embrace the challenge as they begin with a daunting trip to champions Northampton Saints on Friday night.

"It couldn't be set up any better for a spectacle for us," McFarland said. "The team starting at the back of the grid against the team on pole position.

"For us, it's a massive challenge and exactly the sort of thing a Red Bull team would relish going after, something that's hugely tough but really exciting to be involved in."

Englishman McFarland has returned home to head up that challenge after a successful spell in Japan as forwards coach at Kobelco Kobe Steelers.

The Red Bulls had three different head coaches last season with Steve Diamond, Alan Dickens and then Stephen Jones in charge but McFarland feels like the first proper appointment by the new ownership for this role.

"One of the reasons this was so attractive was trying to pull something together from scratch, basically being a start-up," he said.

Previously head coach at Ulster, the 54-year-old has got used to big business and rugby working together and he has tapped into the Red Bull organisation in his first few months on Tyneside.

Newcastle have recruited no fewer than 25 new players for this season so gelling that number of people together in a few weeks presents a significant obstacle.

But he reveals they benefited from a trip to the organisation's headquarters in Salzburg in Austria in pre-season to help a new playing squad gel and feel part of a wider family.

"Outside of Japan, big corporations don't get involved in rugby clubs," said McFarland.

"It's very rare, to have that backing but it's also the way Red Bull go into these kinds of ventures. It's not a feeling of 'let's see how it goes'. It's in with two feet and 'we've deliberately chosen you, Newcastle, because we believe we can do special things with you'.

"That is pretty special and they back it up with the support, the opportunities they offer for collaboration at different levels within the organisation - it could be for athlete performance teams, elite athletes and definitely in marketing."

After their opener at Northampton, Newcastle then face two other play-off sides from last season - a home game with Leicester Tigers and a trip to Exeter Chiefs - in the opening three-week block of league fixtures.

It is not an easy start, but McFarland likens Newcastle's challenge in the Prem this season to that undertaken by Red Bull's F1 driver Max Verstappen as he raced behind 100 amateur drivers in a go-kart race at Silverstone earlier this month - slightly eccentric but one that gets the juices flowing.

"We look at it like this, we're starting at the back of the grid and we've got all these teams ahead of us," he said.

"Let's see if we can pick them off and we're going to have fun trying to do it."

title: Contagious, confident - the rise of Lewis Koumas
description: Having made his mark in the early stages of the season at Liverpool, Lewis Koumas will aim to continue his good form with Wales in the Nations League.
fullText:
It took less than a week of pre-season for the 21-year-old to show new Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola what he could offer.

And it has taken less than a month of the new season for him to show why he has a place in Liverpool's plans.

Now, over the next fortnight, the attacking prospect who is fast becoming an Anfield favourite will attempt to prove what several people in Welsh football have suspected for a long while - that he can have a big impact on the international stage too.

"I feel he's going to be a really important player for us for a number of years," Wales boss Craig Bellamy said before Nations League games with Portugal, Denmark and Norway that will see Koumas share an international stage with the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo and Erling Haaland.

Thursday, 24 September, 19:45 BST

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Bellamy is not alone. Wales and Liverpool legend Ian Rush is among a growing number impressed by Koumas' potential, a potential that – despite his recent rise to prominence – has been obvious for a number of years.

Right from the off, in fact. The surname alone brought excitement, given the talents of Lewis' father, former Wales international Jason Koumas.

"Jason was a talented, talented player," says Danny Gabbidon, who played alongside the older Koumas for Wales.

"He could do a bit of everything; technically amazing, he could look after the ball, pass, score fantastic goals. He could just make things happen."

The phrase mercurial midfielder never felt more fitting than for Koumas senior, who won 34 caps and scored 10 goals for Wales but could delight and frustrate in equal measure.

"He could be a bit lazy at times," chuckles Gabbidon when considering a player who was often nonchalance personified.

Indeed, Tranmere Rovers, West Bromwich Albion, Cardiff City and Wigan Athletic fans will all smile at the highlight-reel memories, while having a nagging feeling of what might have been had Koumas had the tenacity to match his talent.

Yet it seems Lewis has some of the qualities his father may have lacked.

"You wouldn't have seen Jason running around like Lewis the other night [for Liverpool against Tottenham] ," says Gabbidon.

"I kept a close eye on him because I've felt his best position is a striker and I've been keen to see him down the middle.

"To get the chance at a club like Liverpool shows what the manager thinks of him. But it's not just his talent, it's the appetite."

Name Wales' Euro 2016 semi-final XI against Ronaldo's Portugal

The younger Koumas' attitude is something that has been noted for some time.

Former Liverpool Under-21 head coach Barry Lewtas describes him as "a coach's dream".

"The effort, the will to learn and develop, how he applies himself, it's all there," Lewtas says.

A Liverpool supporter from birth, Koumas has been with the Reds since primary school age, following in the footsteps of his father, who was once a nine-year-old team-mate of Steven Gerrard and Michael Owen.

While Jason moved on to Tranmere without making the breakthrough at Liverpool, Lewis has flourished with the Premier League giants, especially since being pushed from midfield into a forward role at the age of 16.

"That was an important part of his development, getting that exposure of playing deeper, dealing with the ball and the technical side," adds Lewtas.

"But then, when your skill-sets develop, you find the area that suits you best."

Given the influence of then Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp, Lewtas says Koumas' finishing prowess combined with a ferocious attitude towards pressing meant his path was obvious.

"He fitted us and we fitted him," Lewtas says.

He scored in the FA Cup against Southampton in February 2024 was then an unused substitute as Liverpool beat Chelsea to win the League Cup at Wembley.

There were more than 900 days before his next first-team appearance for Liverpool, with three loan spells in the Championship in between.

At Stoke City, Koumas played under three different managers in a single season, but earned roles under all three during a spell credited for boosting his belief.

He played 25 times for Birmingham City in the first half last season - though managed only seven league starts - before moving on to Hull City and playing an important role in the Tigers' promotion via the play-offs.

Koumas returned to Liverpool in the summer with renewed confidence.

The assumption was that another loan spell beckoned, but Iraola put a stop to such thoughts a week into the club's pre-season trip to the United States.

A Premier League debut followed, as did a first appearance in the Champions League, plus a relentless man-of-the-match performance against Tottenham that enamoured him to the Anfield crowd and seemed to symbolise the demands of the club's new boss.

How to follow Wales in the Nations League on the BBC

"He's really matured since making his debut," says Theo Squires, senior football writer at the Liverpool Echo.

"Back then he was just a boy who had caught the eye at academy level as a versatile forward with a keen eye for goal.

"He looks almost unrecognisable physically. Leading the line against Tottenham, he more than held his own and he was a constant nuisance with his pace and never-say-die pressing."

Koumas' energy was described by Iraola as being contagious for the rest of the Liverpool squad, £100m-plus signings included.

"It's been brilliant to see," adds Lewtas. "But it's not just a case of running about and working hard, it's his intelligence. He doesn't just understand what to do, but why he's doing it."

Koumas knows what he is capable of, too.

Matty Jones, the Wales Under-21 head coach, has spoken of the regular meetings he had with Koumas to ensure there was no chance of England nabbing the Wirral-born Welshman.

One ended with Koumas telling Jones: "I'll win you games".

A match-winning, curling finish on his international under-21 debut in 2025 backed up the quiet self-assurance.

Before last June's senior international friendlies, Koumas said Wales fans had not seen "anything from me yet".

He pointed that having played only cameo roles for Wales, he needed to "work harder and show a little bit more to get the trust of the gaffer".

He duly scored his first international goal against Ghana.

"He's been there in every squad I've announced but I felt in the summer, he turned," says Bellamy. "When he came on against Ghana, he changed it completely – and he's a player who's capable of that.

"He's just coming into his own now and kicking on again – and to be the top player we expect him to be, that has to be the case."

Both club and international bosses agree there is more to work on, but also that there is more to come.

Wales will hope that he can make further strides during a demanding Nations League campaign which begins against Portugal in Lisbon on Thursday.

"He knows there is a higher ceiling," says Lewtas.

"Knowing Lewis' appetite for things, he won't be worried about it, he'll be looking forward to it."

title: How Premier League teams have really started - according to xG
description: Which Premier League teams have overperformed their xG and who has underperformed?
fullText:
How have Premier League teams really started?

At this stage last season Liverpool were top, with five wins out of five, and Tottenham were third. Given that they finished fifth and 17th respectively, it shows that the table shouldn't be taken too seriously this early on.

While any statistics should be taken with a pinch of salt - given such a small sample size of games and the fact that some teams have had more difficult starts than others - they do provide a more accurate picture of how the season could unfold.

Expected goals (xG) tells us how much teams have dominated games, based on the number and quality of shots they've taken and faced. Basically, how well they've performed in general before finishing, shot-stopping and plain old luck come into play.

And Premier League history shows us that the more a team dominates games, the more points they win in the long run.

It's best to exclude penalties as refereeing decisions and defensive clumsiness give a false impression of how good teams actually are at attacking and defending, especially at this early stage.

Champions Arsenal may have suffered their biggest defeat in three years last weekend at Brighton but they've still been the best team overall based on xG difference.

Leaders Manchester City are not too far behind them in terms of how much they've dominated their games, while there's nothing fortunate about unbeaten Brentford's impressive start to the season.

Manchester United constantly seem to flip between feast and famine, when often they've simply been fine. Despite their underwhelming start, only three teams have a higher xG difference so far.

The likes of Nottingham Forest and Bournemouth have also been better than their position in the early table suggests.

At the other end, Aston Villa, Crystal Palace and Newcastle have been the least impressive in terms of their overall performance, with the latter perhaps the most surprising given their position in the top half.

It's still early days, so there's no need to panic just yet, but it shows that those teams have a lot of room to improve - something Villa did to great effect after a slow start last season by finishing fourth.

Worryingly for the established sides though, the promoted teams seem like they won't be going down without a fight, with both Hull and Ipswich making genuinely solid starts to the campaign.

Looking at teams' numbers going forward, Brighton have the best attack so far based on the number and quality of chances they've had, followed by Manchester City, Brentford and Manchester United.

Although the Gunners are more admired for their defensive prowess, it's still surprising that eight teams have a higher xG than champions Arsenal, while Liverpool and Chelsea also rank in mid-table.

Brighton not only have the highest xG but have also been one of the most ruthless sides in front of goal, scoring 15 non-penalty goals from their 10.7 xG.

The only team to be more clinical than the Seagulls is their avian cousins the Magpies, who actually have the lowest xG in the league so far.

Newcastle have scored twice as many goals as a team historically would given the chances they've had - 9 goals from 4.5 xG - but head coach Matthias Jaissle will no doubt want his team to create more and not have to rely on such sharp finishing as the season goes on.

In contrast, Coventry, Sunderland, Nottingham Forest and Tottenham have all scored three goals fewer than they really should have given the opportunities they've had in their first five games.

It'll be interesting to see whether those teams genuinely have a problem with their finishing or if their luck in front of goal simply begins to change in the games to come.

As mentioned earlier, champions Arsenal are renowned for their defence and they still have by far the best backline in the league - even taking their heavy defeat by Brighton into account.

While Forest head coach Oliver Glasner has work to do to get his side scoring goals, he's already instilled a solid foundation to build from at the back, as has Andoni Iraola at Liverpool.

There's a lot of construction work needed in the capital as Crystal Palace, Fulham and Chelsea have all been far too open at the back so far this season, although Xabi Alonso's side are not quite as terrible as the 12 goals they've conceded suggests.

Brighton's brilliance going forward has come at the cost of them not being particularly solid in defence, with Fabian Hurzeler's team perhaps a little fortunate not to have conceded more often.

Everton and Leeds have also conceded three goals fewer than expected given the chances they've faced, although both sides have been among the strongest defensively overall.

Just five games into the new campaign, it's too early to be making any concrete claims about how sides will perform but their underlying numbers have given us a glimpse of what might be in store this season.

title: Edwards' Red Roses move inspired by late mother
description: England back row Marlie Packer says defence coach Shaun Edwards' surprise move into the Red Roses set-up was partly inspired by his late mother Phyllis.
fullText:
England back row Marlie Packer says defence coach Shaun Edwards' surprise move into the Red Roses set-up was partly inspired by his late mother Phyllis.

Edwards has joined the world champions for the remainder of their autumn campaign after the end of a six-and-a half-year stint with France.

"He told us a little story, telling us why he wanted to be here," said Packer.

"He was saying about his mum not ever being able to have the opportunity to play, and that she would have loved to have done so.

"It was really cool to hear that she thought we were amazing."

Phyllis Edwards worked as a hairdresser in the family's hometown of Wigan, but was a trusted advisor throughout her son's career. She also cared for Edwards' father Jackie after his own career with league side Warrington was ended by a spinal injury at the age of 24.

"Back in the mid-1990s she was the first person to tell me to study rugby union as well as rugby league, because I always wanted to be a coach and I always took notes of what coaches said," said Edwards at the time.

"When rugby union went professional in 1995, I was at the top of the league game, captain of Wigan who were world champions, but she always told me to learn about rugby union."

Edwards' study paid off. After lifting domestic and European titles during his time coaching club side Wasps, he has won a total of seven Six Nations crowns across stints with Wales and France.

"He's got more Six Nations than quite a few of the girls, to be fair to him!" added Packer, who has been part of 10 Grand Slam-winning sides herself since making her England debut in 2008.

"To have that calibre of coach to want to come and work with the Red Roses, just showcases where the women's game is going and what this Red Roses team has done and are doing.

"It's amazing for the whole programme.

"He's straight talking. He doesn't say too much, but when he does say something, you hear it."

England's winning run was halted on 39 successive Tests last weekend, when Canada held them to a 26-26 draw at Sandy Park.

England take on New Zealand, the Red Roses' closest challengers at the top of the world rankings, at Allianz Stadium on Saturday, before crossing the Atlantic next month for matches against Canada in Ottawa and Toronto, and a Test against the United States.

"We're not happy with the draw, but we didn't lose a match," said Packer.

"It was a really great game of rugby. If you're a neutral that's the kind of rugby that you want to come and watch - you don't know who's going to win, end-to-end scoring, and such a physical, physical game.

"We know we have to build from last week. We're in a Test series against Canada; that's our first game, now we've got two away legs. We know what we have got to put right."

Saturday, 26 September, 15:00 BST

Live on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentary

The WXV Global Series - the new event designed to increase the number and competitiveness of Test matches in the autumn for the world's best women - has delivered several superb games.

In addition to England's draw against Canada, last weekend featured France recovering from 19 points down to beat Australia 29-26 and the United States overhauling a 17-point deficit to see off Ireland 40-36 in Dublin.

Australia also came hard at England on the opening weekend of matches, leading 10-5 at half-time in Salford before succumbing to a 48-15 defeat.

"The Red Roses are always pushing that bar higher, then it's for the other teams to raise their game, that's exactly what's happening and that's what we want as players," Packer added.

"The more the game goes professional, the more the unions put money into their women's sides, we're going to see better contests of rugby.

"We're going to see that the Red Roses have it won in the first half. There will have to be 80-minute performances.

"We don't want to turn up and have to have targets within games because we know we're going to win. We want to be in a rugby contest."

The Black Ferns were the last team to beat England, upsetting them in the Women's Rugby World Cup final at Eden Park in November 2022.

They come into Saturday's contest under the leadership of Whitney Hansen, who has won all seven Tests since taking over as head coach in December, including a 36-14 victory over Canada in April in Kansas.

title: From leaving Rangers to La Liga - Scotland is next step for Ure
description: Robbie Ure has made it all the way to Sevilla since failing to break through at Rangers and now a first Scotland cap awaits the striker, writes Tom English.
fullText:
Robbie Ure, cool and confident and 22 years old, played 90 minutes for Sevilla against Barcelona at the weekend; 90 minutes of being marked by Pau Cubarsi, man of the match in the World Cup final, 90 minutes of pitch-time with Rodri, player of the tournament, 90 minutes of breathing the same rarefied air as Lamine Yamal.

Ure is a part of a new-ish wave of Scotland striker, uncapped but hopeful of making a debut on Saturday away to Slovenia in the Nations League.

There is no Lyndon Dykes in Sebastien Pocognoli's squad and no George Hirst. Injury has ruled out Che Adams, Lawrence Shankland and Ross Stewart. Those five were all at the World Cup in the United States during the summer.

Now, it's Ure alongside James Wilson of Hearts and Kieron Bowie of Sassuolo, who both have two caps, and Oli McBurnie of Hull, with the last of his 16 international appearances coming five years ago.

There is an intriguing freshness to this and nowhere is that buzz more obvious than in the story of Ure, the boy who wanted to play for Rangers but couldn't force his way in, the young man who in his seven games for Sevilla since his move from IK Sirius in Sweden has already played against 12 of Spain's World Cup winning squad.

Just over three years ago, Ure left Rangers as a teenager, his last forays with the senior team being one minute against St Mirren in November 2022 and another minute against Hibs in May 2023.

Nations League: Slovenia v Scotland

He is the poster boy in the Scottish FA's campaign to persuade clubs to give youth more of a chance. Ure wasn't given that opportunity in Glasgow and left for Anderlecht, then IK Sirius and now Sevilla, who paid £5.5m for him, plus another £2.5m in add-ons.

He calls the past few months "busy" which is an understatement. He's operating at a different level now. Sevilla lost that Barcelona game 3-1 - he has yet to score for his new club - but this is an education he's receiving, a critical part of his development.

"The first half, we were good," he says. "But as the game goes on, they wear you down. Raphinha at the moment. I mean…"

There's a knowing smile there, an indication of the kind of class he is now witnessing. "I really enjoyed it," he adds. "But against these players, you give them one chance and most of the time it's a goal. For me, it was a really good experience. I'm only going to get better as a result of it."

Ure is a Rangers boy - one that got away. Was it difficult having to leave? "Yeah, it was," he explains. "All I'd ever known was Rangers. Going in every single day since I was probably eight years old but it was something that I felt I had to do.

"I felt like I wasn't good enough to play for Rangers at the time, which is normal for many 18-year-olds. It was nothing that affected my confidence. I would have loved to have stayed but I knew myself that I wasn't going to play, which I accepted.

"At a club like Rangers, it's difficult for any 18-year-old to play. I needed a change of scenery and a fresh start, somewhere that I could go to play at a level that would be good enough for me at the time. Anderlecht provided that."

Well-travelled Binks eager to make mark for Scotland

McPake's 'colourful' journey from club-less to Scotland call-up in three years

Belgium was the first step on his road to the Scotland team but Sweden was when it all started to happen. In 2025-26, he scored 11 goals in 30 games, a mere warm-up for what was to follow.

Between April and July this year, Ure played 14 games for IK Sirius and scored 15 goals, including four in one game against Mjallby.

"I was scoring near enough every game, so that was probably the happiest I've been," he says. "Every week I was scoring and we were top of the league. I was improving and that interest in me was getting bigger and bigger.

"At a young age it's really important you're playing. I was playing 90 minutes every week, getting trust from the manager and from the club. I was given time as well. The day I scored the four goals, it was my first hat-trick. I felt like every time I shot it was going to be a goal. I've not had a feeling like that before in football. It was pretty special."

Player pathway is a hot topic in Scottish football and Ure is an example of what can happen when a kid is given a proper chance.

"Everyone's different," he says. "You have to give players patience and give them time to develop but the way to do that is, of course, playing minutes at a level where you can develop at. I couldn't find that level in Scotland, so I had to look elsewhere and I'm happy that I did that."

The level he has found in Spain is stratospheric. No goals yet, but it's a savagely tough school.

He will have his moment under Pocognoli in the coming weeks. Four games in quick succession - he will get his first cap and his first chance to shine on another stage. And he's earned it.

title: MLS coach sacked after sexist remark to female referee
description: MLS club Columbus Crew sack their reserve team coach after he refused to let go of a female referee's hand and says "don't forget this is a man's game".
fullText:
Major League Soccer club Columbus Crew have sacked their reserve team coach after he refused to let go of a female referee's hand and said "don't forget this is a man's game".

Federico Higuain, brother of former Real Madrid striker Gonzalo Higuain, was sent off and given a two-match suspension for the incident during an MLS Next Pro league match.

"We determined it's in the best interest of our club, players and support staff to dismiss Federico Higuain from his responsibilities," Crew general manager Issa Tall said in a statement.

"After conversations this week and further assessing the past month, our club's standards of what's expected from a leader for one of our teams have not been met."

Meanwhile, the Professional Soccer Referees Association (PSRA) criticised the league's response, saying Higuain's two-game ban "falls drastically short".

A statement from the referees' union added: "A male head coach committed two deliberate acts of physical abuse and sexism against a female official - squeezing her hand and refusing to let go after being told to stop three times.

"This physical intimidation was compounded by a demeaning, sexist remark to the official: 'Don't forget, this is a man's game.'

"Women make every level of this game better. They should not have to endure intimidation or degrading comments to prove it.

"Our female officials have proven their excellence on the world stage. They deserve the same respect, dignity, and safe working environment as every other official."

title: Scots recall Kerr & Thomas for World Cup play-offs
description: Sam Kerr and Martha Thomas are named in their first Scotland squad in almost a year for next month's World Cup round one play-offs against the Czech Republic.
fullText:
Sam Kerr and Martha Thomas have been named in their first Scotland squad in almost a year, as the experienced duo return for next month's Women's World Cup round one two-legged play-off against the Czech Republic.

Melissa Andreatta's side travel to Pardubice, east of Prague, on Friday, 9 October before welcoming the Czechs to St Mirren Park four days later, eyeing progression to another two-legged play-off against either Sweden or Lithuania with a place at next summer's tournament in Brazil at stake.

Liverpool midfielder Kerr - who has been playing out of position at right-back in the WSL - has yet to feature under Scotland women's Australian head coach, with the last of her 34 caps coming in February 2025 off the bench against the Netherlands, while Thomas - who joined WSL2 side Newcastle United in the summer - earned her 50th cap in October, in a friendly defeat by Switzerland.

Club-mate Freya Gregory - and Como defender Sophie Howard - who were forced to pull out of the last camp for the qualifying double-header against Israel, are also back in the squad.

Celtic midfielder, Maria McAneny - who last featured when scoring in a seven-goal thrashing of Luxembourg in March, returns too.

Defenders Leah Eddie and Kenzie Weir drop out, as do strikers Eilidh Adams and Laura Berry.

Mia McAulay was a late addition for the June double-header, but the Aston Villa youngster retains her place.

Andreatta's unbeaten side topped their qualifying group on goal difference - one better off than second-placed Belgium - and are now four games away from their first major tournament since the 2019 World Cup, having missed the past two European Championships and the 2023 World Cup.

title: Germany's saviour? How Klopp is looking to turn fortunes around
description: As Jurgen Klopp prepares for his first game as Germany manager, BBC Sport looks at how is trying to turn their fortunes around.
fullText:
It has been quite the ride since Jurgen Klopp was announced as Germany's head coach in July.

In his first news conference, Klopp admonished the media, urging them to treat him fairly and refrain from any attacks against his family.

Last Thursday, during another media conference, Klopp called for "positive patriotism" amid political turmoil in the country.

When asked whether he considers himself an ambassador for Germany in his new role, Klopp's answer was a serious one.

"From my perspective as a sportsman, I can say that I would very much like to reclaim the flag for myself, for all of us," said Klopp.

"I want it so that when someone waves it, no-one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?' Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country."

His statement was made in light of the success of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The anti-immigration party has since scored another win in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Klopp's remarks were widely and positively discussed in the media - the German national team represents a diverse Germany, as several players come from a migrant background.

KIopp also remarked about the recent success of Alexander Zverev at the US Open, the women's basketball team at the European Championship and German athletes at the European Athletics Championships, saying sport can ensure "a sense of community".

He added: "This is our mission: we need to create a good atmosphere."

Klopp knows, intentionally or not, how to make headlines.

However, the German Football Association (DFB) didn't hire the former Liverpool boss on an annual salary of £6m to become a commentator on the state of Germany - but to transform a floundering national team.

Klopp wants to 'reclaim' flag amid German elections

Klopp starts Germany reign by threatening to quit

Between the two news conferences, Klopp looked like the busiest national team boss on the planet, making countless visits to league games and training facilities.

One day fans could see Klopp sitting in the stands of Dortmund's Signal Iduna Park, his old stomping ground and, not long after, they may have caught a picture of him in the VIP lounge of Mainz's stadium or somewhere near Eintracht Frankfurt's training pitch talking to players.

Klopp has approached this new job with open eyes. Initially, the charismatic 59-year-old drew up a list of 57 players who could have been selected for this first international break.

"Players will receive chances who don't even expect it yet," Klopp said in July.

His first selection wasn't short of surprises. In the flavour of a trial-and-error principle, Klopp and his staff decided to select two almost completely different squads for the upcoming four games.

The first squad, including Joshua Kimmich, Kai Havertz and Jamal Musiala, will face arch-rivals the Netherlands at Johan Cruyff Arena on Thursday (19:45 BST) and host Greece on Sunday.

The second squad, with Florian Wirtz and Aleksandar Pavlovic, face Serbia at home and Greece on the road in the second half of this international break. The only player who was selected for both is back-up goalkeeper Finn Dahmen.

The selection process means we will not see Germany's best starting XI this time around. Instead, Klopp clearly intends to try out new players, some of whom played in Germany's second tier only a few months ago.

Take, for example, Felix Keidel, a 23-year-old full-back-midfielder hybrid from recently promoted SV Elversberg.

A year ago, Keidel was as far away from the national team as the Oktoberfest from Rio Carnival.

Now Keidel - just like Mika Baur, Bambase Conte, Max Rosenfelder, Philipp Treu, and Vitaly Janelt - has the chance to show he could be a valuable cog in the machine.

Klopp has never built his success merely on star names - he has always taken a liking to undervalued and overlooked players.

He once signed an little-known Polish winger by the name of Lukasz Piszczek and moulded him into one of the best right-backs in Europe who would go toe-to-toe with Cristiano Ronaldo in his prime. And he helped transform Andy Robertson into a force on Liverpool's left side.

Klopp's style helps to elevate all the members of his squad - not just the most talented.

Fitness and mental readiness are highly important, and some newcomers might just have that to impress the new manager.

But man-marking is prevalent in Germany's top flight, while Klopp prefers his teams to close down the player in possession to create superior numbers around the ball. So some of the Bundesliga players will have to adapt quickly.

"It is not important who plays but how someone plays," Klopp said last week. "I expect a lot from the beginning. It could be a bit wild, but I accept that. It just has to be lively."

Klopp has chosen younger squads compared to the ones we saw in the past couple of years. Manuel Neuer, Antonio Rudiger and Pascal Gross have retired from international football, and other 30-somethings might just not receive a chance to get into the team again.

"I think it is about time to wish the new generation best of luck," Gross said after Brighton's win over Arsenal on Saturday. "I still enjoy playing football here in the club, but there's a change in Germany and rightfully so."

Both squads for this international break have an average age between 24 and 25. Youth and energy seem to be preferred.

"I have the desire to work with guys who cannot wait to wear this jersey, who want to play the kind of football everybody enjoys and who perform even better wearing the national team jersey," Klopp said.

We can expect from him to simplify Germany's approach to ball possession. Predecessor Julian Nagelsmann bent over backwards to hide some of the flaws he detected in his squad and thus created highly complex tactical systems.

On the contrary, Klopp intends to put an emphasis on the wings and break defences there. We saw what he was able to achieve with the likes of Mohamed Salah, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Sadio Mane from wide areas.

While underwhelming at the past couple of international tournaments, Germany still possess a deep talent pool. Cologne's rising star Said El Mala and 18-year-old Bayern Munich talent Lennart Karl will get chances to show their skills on the wings.

Freiburg's Derry Scherhant and Barcelona's Karim Adeyemi provide plenty of speed, just like Brentford's Kevin Schade who has returned to the squad after being left out for the World Cup. There is potential for an exciting Germany side we have not seen in quite a while.

Finally, the emotional component plays a role in Klopp's entire approach. He works towards a fresh start for the national team and a new spirit in the country.

Last Thursday, he wore a cap that read "One of 83 million". It was a clear indication he wants to unite all 83 million Germans behind this team and they are all in it together.

Klopp has spent plenty of time thus far attempting to shape narratives off the field - but now the spotlight turns to his ability to get the best out of his group of players on the pitch.
